paragraphs: This paper proposes a way to mark language-model output so that an algorithm can recognize the mark even when a person reading the text cannot. The framework targets proprietary language models and separates the ability to generate marked text from the ability to detect it. Detection does not require access to the model’s parameters or API.

Before generating a word, the method randomly selects a set of preferred, or green, tokens. It then gently increases the chance of selecting those tokens during sampling. Rather than inserting an explicit label into the text, this process creates a statistical pattern across the generated tokens. The authors describe a statistical detection test that reports interpretable p-values.

The paper also develops an information-theoretic analysis of detection sensitivity and tests the framework with a multi-billion-parameter OPT model. It reports that the watermark can have negligible impact on text quality and can be detected efficiently from a short token span. Robustness and security are discussed, without a claim that detection is guaranteed under every modification.
icml-2023-a-watermark-for-large-language.tldr: Softly favoring randomized token sets creates a statistical watermark that can be detected without access to the generating language model.

paragraphs: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, exploration is a decision for every agent, and the useful amount can change during learning. This paper introduces ADER, a framework that learns an exploration target for each agent. It focuses on entropy-based exploration, where greater policy entropy corresponds to a wider spread of possible action choices.

The central step is to separate the soft value function into a component measuring return and another measuring entropy. The authors then apply multi-agent value factorization to the return component. This yields a metric based on how the pure-return value changes with an individual agent’s policy entropy. That sensitivity provides a basis for determining how much exploration is relevant for each agent.

ADER uses this metric within maximum-entropy reinforcement learning to learn individual target entropies over time. The approach therefore connects exploration levels to their relationship with return, rather than treating exploration as a single shared quantity. Experiments report significant improvements over current state-of-the-art multi-agent reinforcement-learning algorithms in the evaluated settings.
icml-2023-an-adaptive-entropy-regulariza.tldr: ADER adapts each agent’s exploration by learning target entropies from how exploration relates to collective return.

paragraphs: Large-dataset pretraining can give a neural network a useful starting point, but the resources it requires are concentrated in relatively few communities. This paper investigates a different way to supply that starting point: train one neural network to predict the parameters of other networks. The goal is to make the benefits of pretraining more accessible.

The authors train and release a single parameter-prediction network that produces high-quality ImageNet parameters for diverse models. Those predictions are used to initialize the receiving networks before further training. The reported benefit is therefore about improving where training begins. A shared predictor can provide useful initial parameters across different models, rather than being limited to supplying a starting point for one network.

For diverse ImageNet models available in PyTorch, the predicted initializations improve training. The authors also transfer initialized models to other datasets, where they converge faster and achieve competitive final performance. These findings support parameter prediction as a practical route toward sharing pretraining benefits, with both training speed and the quality of the resulting models contributing to its usefulness.
icml-2023-can-we-scale-transformers-to-p.tldr: A single network predicts useful initial parameters for diverse ImageNet models, accelerating training and transfer to other datasets.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders can suffer from posterior collapse: the distribution inferred from an input becomes the same as the prior distribution. In that situation, the inferred representation does not capture the input’s latent structure. This paper addresses how to control the degree of that collapse, rather than simply treating it as an all-or-nothing outcome.

The proposed intervention is architectural. The authors place an inverse Lipschitz neural network in the decoder, the part of the model that maps latent representations toward generated data. An inverse Lipschitz constraint limits how much differences between latent inputs can be compressed by that mapping. This gives the decoder a controlled sensitivity to changes in the latent representation.

Building on this decoder design, the paper presents a method for controlling posterior collapse across a wide range of VAE models, supported by a concrete theoretical guarantee. Several numerical experiments also illustrate its effectiveness. The contribution is a direct connection between a property of the decoder and control over collapse, giving the architectural constraint an explicit role in preserving informative latent structure.
icml-2023-controlling-posterior-collapse.tldr: An inverse Lipschitz constraint on a VAE decoder provides theoretically supported control over the degree of posterior collapse.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents need exploration that produces useful experience. One approach uses options: policies followed for an extended period rather than selecting each exploratory action independently. This paper develops a scalable way to discover options from the eigenfunctions of a graph Laplacian, mathematical objects used by earlier methods to organize exploration.

Previous Laplacian-based approaches were mostly restricted to tabular environments. They depended on having or fully estimating the Laplacian matrix, being able to compute its eigendecomposition, and learning value functions exactly. They also required a separate phase for discovering options. Together, these requirements made it difficult to apply the approach to larger problems with complex observations.

The authors use results for directly approximating Laplacian eigenfunctions to build a fully online deep reinforcement-learning algorithm. Option discovery can therefore occur during ongoing learning without a separate discovery phase. Evaluations on multiple tasks with pixel observations compare the method against leading exploration approaches. The results support its effectiveness and generality, with particularly promising findings in settings that change over time.
icml-2023-deep-laplacian-based-options-f.tldr: An online deep reinforcement-learning method scales Laplacian-based exploratory options to pixel-based tasks, with promising results in changing environments.

paragraphs: Generating an image with a diffusion model can require many steps of a reverse stochastic or ordinary differential equation. Much work speeds up the numerical integration of that equation. Denoising MCMC takes a complementary approach: it changes the starting points supplied to the integrator, reducing how much denoising those points need.

The method first runs Markov chain Monte Carlo in a space that includes both the data and diffusion time. It then applies a reverse-equation integrator to the resulting initialization points. Because the MCMC process moves near the data manifold, producing a clean sample from these points costs much less than starting from noise.

The tested instance, Denoising Langevin Gibbs, accelerates all six integrators considered. On CIFAR10, it achieves FID values of 3.25 with approximately 10 score evaluations and 2.49 with approximately 16. On CelebA-HQ-256, it achieves 6.99 FID with approximately 160 evaluations, compared with the cited prior score-based result of 7.16 using 4,000. These findings show that better initialization can complement improvements to the integrator itself.
icml-2023-denoising-mcmc-for-acceleratin.tldr: Denoising MCMC accelerates diffusion sampling by supplying starting points near the data manifold before numerical denoising.

paragraphs: Drug-discovery prediction often combines two difficulties: few labeled examples and a mismatch between the chemical inputs available for training and those encountered later. This mismatch, called covariate shift, makes extrapolation challenging for standard deep-learning methods. The paper introduces Q-SAVI to incorporate relevant prior knowledge into predictions in this setting.

Q-SAVI is a probabilistic model that places a prior distribution over functions. This allows knowledge about the data-generating process to express preferences about the predictive relationships the model should consider plausible. The approach makes those preferences explicit and probabilistically grounded. In the reported application, the prior incorporates contextual knowledge about the space of drug-like chemicals.

The authors build a new bioactivity dataset and investigate ways to induce data shift, creating an evaluation focused on extrapolation. In that setup, Q-SAVI delivers substantial improvements in predictive accuracy and calibration over a broad range of self-supervised pretraining and domain-adaptation approaches. The results support using domain-informed priors to improve both predictions and their associated confidence when labeled data are scarce and inputs shift.
icml-2023-drug-discovery-under-covariate.tldr: Q-SAVI encodes chemical-domain knowledge in function priors to improve bioactivity prediction and calibration under data scarcity and covariate shift.

paragraphs: Treatment effects can differ across people, so a policy that assigns treatments needs information about those differences. This paper proposes a general framework for estimating such heterogeneous effects while imposing fairness constraints. Its nonparametric approach addresses the estimation problem without fixing a particular finite-dimensional formula for how treatment effects vary.

A central theoretical result is that the resulting estimators have the double robustness property under standard regularity conditions. This gives the framework a robustness guarantee alongside its fairness constraints. The qualification matters: the stated result depends on those regularity conditions. Fairness and statistical robustness are therefore considered together within the estimation framework, rather than being evaluated as entirely separate concerns.

The authors then use the framework to characterize a trade-off between fairness and the greatest welfare an optimal policy can achieve. This connects constraints on estimation to the quality of decisions made using those estimates. A simulation study evaluates the methods, and a real-world case study illustrates their use. The contribution combines a general estimation framework, a conditional robustness result, and an analysis of the welfare consequences of fairness requirements.
icml-2023-fair-and-robust-estimation-of-.tldr: A fairness-constrained treatment-effect framework provides conditional double robustness and characterizes the trade-off between fairness and achievable policy welfare.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering organizes data into nested groups, so fairness can matter at multiple levels of the resulting hierarchy. This paper studies how to obtain fair hierarchical clusterings while controlling their cost. It evaluates that cost using Dasgupta’s objective, providing a theoretical measure for assessing the price of enforcing fairness.

The main result improves a previous fair approximation guarantee of O(n^(5/6) polylog(n)) to O(n^δ polylog(n)) for any constant δ between zero and one. Allowing a smaller fixed exponent substantially improves the dependence of the guarantee on problem size. The bound retains its n^δ factor, even though the paper describes the resulting approximation as near polylogarithmic.

The analysis establishes a trade-off between clustering cost and fairness and accommodates broader fairness constraints than the previous work. The authors also show how to modify existing hierarchical clusterings so that fairness and cluster balance are guaranteed across any level of the hierarchy. This makes the contribution useful both as an improved approximation result and as a way to adapt clusterings that have already been constructed.
icml-2023-generalized-reductions-making-.tldr: The paper improves fair hierarchical-clustering cost guarantees and shows how to enforce fairness and balance throughout existing hierarchies.

paragraphs: A Differentiable Search Index stores information about a document collection inside a neural network’s parameters and maps queries directly to documents. Although this approach has achieved strong retrieval performance, adding documents after training is difficult. IncDSI addresses this update problem so that the collection represented by the network can grow in real time.

The method formulates each document addition as a constrained optimization problem. Its objective is to make minimal changes to the network parameters while incorporating the new document. This replaces retraining on the full dataset, or even a subset of it, with a targeted parameter update. The constraint-based formulation makes document insertion an explicit operation on the learned index.

The authors report update times of approximately 20–50 milliseconds per document. Their approach is orders of magnitude faster than retraining on the whole dataset while remaining competitive in retrieval performance. These findings support the practical possibility of maintaining a neural document index as new information arrives, rather than treating the trained index as a largely fixed representation of its original collection.
icml-2023-incdsi-incrementally-updatable.tldr: IncDSI adds documents to a neural search index through small constrained updates, reporting 20–50 milliseconds per document and competitive retrieval performance.

paragraphs: Class incremental learning asks one model to learn a sequence of tasks whose classes do not overlap. At any point, that model must classify examples from every class encountered so far. Test examples arrive without information identifying their task, so the learner must handle the accumulated classification problem through a single model.

The paper addresses a foundational question about this setting: whether it is learnable. Earlier work had established that a strong system needs both accurate prediction within each task and strong detection of examples outside each task’s distribution. Those capabilities clarify what successful systems require, but they do not by themselves settle the learnability question.

The authors provide a theoretical result establishing learnability for class incremental learning and use that theory to propose a new algorithm. Experiments demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness. The contribution therefore connects an underlying theoretical possibility with a concrete learning method. It gives a formal basis for studying this setting beyond the largely empirical techniques that had motivated the work.
icml-2023-learnability-and-algorithm-for.tldr: The paper establishes learnability for class incremental learning and develops an empirically effective algorithm from the theory.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns a policy from previously collected experience. In a model-based approach, the learner also uses an estimated model, making errors in that model relevant to policy quality. Count-MORL uses estimates of how often state-action pairs occur to determine how conservatively the learned model should be treated.

The paper first shows an inverse relationship between model-estimation error and the frequency of state-action pairs. This connects conservatism to data coverage: less frequently observed pairs provide weaker support for the estimated model. The authors then establish near-optimal performance guarantees for the policy learned using their count-based conservative model. Counts thus provide a common basis for both the algorithm and its theoretical analysis.

For implementation, the method uses hash codes to obtain count estimates. Numerical experiments on D4RL benchmark datasets report significant improvements over existing offline reinforcement-learning algorithms. The authors present this as, to their knowledge, the first demonstration that count-based conservatism is effective in model-based offline deep reinforcement learning. The empirical results support the usefulness of frequency information in the evaluated benchmark settings.
icml-2023-model-based-offline-reinforcem.tldr: Count-MORL uses state-action frequency estimates to guide model conservatism, combining near-optimality guarantees with strong D4RL results.

paragraphs: In online learning with feedback graphs, choosing an action reveals the losses of its neighboring actions as well. The graph therefore determines how much information each choice supplies. This paper studies minimax regret, which measures the best achievable worst-case learning performance, across different graphs and numbers of learning rounds.

A commonly stated regret rate is proportional to the square root of αT, where α is the graph’s independence number and T is the number of rounds. However, the established guarantee applies only when T exceeds α cubed. That restriction can be significant for large graphs, where a learner may operate for fewer rounds than the existing result requires.

The authors introduce a new measure called problem complexity, R*, and prove that minimax regret is proportional to it for any graph and time horizon. They also develop Exp3-EX, whose exploration strategy achieves the optimal regret bound. This supplies both a characterization of the attainable performance and an algorithm that reaches it, including when T is smaller than α cubed.
icml-2023-online-learning-with-feedback-.tldr: A new problem-complexity measure characterizes optimal feedback-graph regret for every time horizon, and Exp3-EX achieves that bound.

paragraphs: Black-box variational inference uses stochastic gradient descent to fit an approximate Bayesian distribution. Understanding how much its gradient estimates fluctuate is important for proving convergence and improving algorithms. This paper addresses a gap between existing analyses of those fluctuations and the conditions used in stochastic-gradient convergence theory.

The authors establish a matching bound corresponding to the ABC condition from the stochastic-gradient literature. The result applies when log-likelihoods are smooth and grow quadratically. These are substantive conditions on the inference problem: they define the setting in which the paper connects gradient variance to the convergence-analysis framework. The contribution supplies a theoretical bridge between BBVI and the optimization method commonly used to train it.

The analysis also extends to nonlinear ways of parameterizing covariance, which are widely used in practical BBVI. In addition, the authors prove that a mean-field parameterization has better dimensional dependence in its variance. This identifies a theoretical advantage in how gradient noise scales with dimension, alongside the broader result connecting practical variational parameterizations to established optimization conditions.
icml-2023-practical-and-matching-gradien.tldr: For smooth, quadratically growing log-likelihoods, BBVI satisfies a matching gradient-variance bound tied to SGD theory, with favorable dimensional scaling for mean-field parameterizations.

paragraphs: Improving a text classifier by collecting more labeled examples can be costly, particularly when the accuracy gains are small. This paper explores adding a different kind of annotation to texts already in a benchmark. It asks for task-specific preferences between pairs of texts, supplying relational information alongside the existing classification labels.

The proposed prefer-to-classify framework, P2C, trains classification and preference prediction together. Individual labels describe each example separately, while pairwise comparisons provide an additional training signal about the relationship between examples. The multi-task setup aims to make these two kinds of supervision cooperate, extracting more useful information from an existing collection of texts.

The authors describe three practical sources of preferences: existing annotation records, explicit judgments from crowd workers, and pretrained language models such as GPT-3. Existing records can supply signals without additional annotation cost but are often unavailable; crowd and language-model annotation have different stated costs. Experiments on existing NLP classification benchmarks show that auxiliary preference learning improves the classifiers, supporting complementary annotation as a useful way to strengthen established datasets.
icml-2023-prefer-to-classify-improving-t.tldr: P2C improves text classifiers by jointly learning classification labels and task-specific pairwise preferences over existing texts.

paragraphs: An observation may not uniquely reveal the latent factors that generated it. A blurred image or a two-dimensional view of a three-dimensional object can be compatible with multiple latent explanations. This paper studies contrastive learning in that ambiguous setting, where uncertainty is inherent in the observation and its amount can differ between inputs.

The authors extend the InfoNCE objective and the encoder so that each input is represented by a probability distribution over latents rather than a single point. In the setup they study, they prove that these predicted distributions recover the correct posterior distributions, including their aleatoric uncertainty. Recovery is defined up to a rotation of the latent space, preserving that qualification on the theoretical result.

These distributions support calibrated uncertainty estimates and credible intervals for image retrieval. A retrieval result can therefore express which images share the query’s latent explanation while accounting for ambiguity in the query itself. The contribution links a probabilistic contrastive objective to recovery of meaningful uncertainty, extending the representation from one latent estimate to a distribution of plausible explanations.
icml-2023-probabilistic-contrastive-lear.tldr: Probabilistic contrastive learning recovers latent posteriors and inherent input uncertainty up to rotation in the studied setup.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to evaluate a discrete generative model when both the model and the target distribution are accessible only through independent samples. It defines a black-box proper loss as one whose expected value is minimized when the generated distribution matches the target. The aim is an evaluation rule that rewards distributional correctness under this restricted access.

Using statistical estimation theory, the authors give a general construction and characterization of such losses. In the sampling setting they analyze, the losses must have a polynomial form, and the number of samples drawn from the model and target must exceed the polynomial’s degree. This connects the structure of a valid loss to the sampling resources needed to compute it.

The characterization rules out a loss whose expectation equals the cross-entropy between the target and model in that setting. However, the authors then extend the construction to more general sampling schemes, including Poisson sampling, and show that such a loss becomes possible. The distinction demonstrates that what can be evaluated depends critically on how sampling is allowed to work.
icml-2023-proper-losses-for-discrete-gen.tldr: The paper characterizes sample-based proper losses for discrete generators and shows how broader sampling schemes enable cross-entropy estimation.

paragraphs: Mirror descent value iteration underlies reinforcement-learning methods using KL or entropy regularization. Despite practical use with function approximation, its theoretical understanding had largely concerned tabular problems. This paper studies its sample requirements with linear function approximation, asking how much data is needed to identify a near-optimal policy with high probability.

The analysis assumes an infinite-horizon linear Markov decision process, access to a generative model, and G-optimal design. Within this setting, the authors identify variance-weighted least-squares regression as crucial to minimax optimality. The weights use the variance of an estimated optimal value function at the next state, making that uncertainty part of the value-estimation procedure.

The resulting VWLS-MDVI algorithm achieves nearly minimax-optimal sample complexity for infinite-horizon linear MDPs. The authors also translate the weighting idea into Deep Variance Weighting, a practical method for value-based deep reinforcement learning. Experiments show improvements to popular algorithms on a set of MinAtar benchmarks. These are complementary contributions: a sample-efficiency guarantee in the specified linear setting and empirical evidence for a related technique in deep RL.
icml-2023-regularization-and-variance-we.tldr: Variance-weighted regression yields nearly minimax-optimal MDVI in the specified linear-MDP setting and improves deep RL performance on MinAtar.

paragraphs: Symmetries describe transformations under which a model’s behavior should change predictably or remain unchanged. Models can build these relationships directly into their architecture, but that can be restrictive when real data follow a symmetry only approximately. This paper considers datasets with several kinds of symmetry, each potentially holding to a different degree.

The method introduces a separate equivariance regularizer for each candidate symmetry type. Each regularizer measures how closely the model follows that symmetry. During training, the method automatically adjusts the strength of these penalties. This lets the model learn how strongly to respect different transformations while also discovering approximation levels for some candidate symmetry types without explicit supervision.

The authors evaluate the approach on synthetic function approximation and motion forecasting. They report better accuracy than prior approaches and correct discovery of approximate symmetry levels. The findings support treating symmetry as something that can be encouraged with adjustable strength. This is useful when several structural patterns coexist in the data but enforcing all of them exactly would impose an overly restrictive model.
icml-2023-regularizing-towards-soft-equi.tldr: Automatically tuned equivariance penalties let models learn different strengths of approximate symmetry, improving accuracy in the reported tasks.

paragraphs: Predicting a reliable characteristic orientation for a three-dimensional point cloud is difficult because shapes in the same class can look very different. This paper aims to obtain orientations that are both stable and consistent by separating the roles of shape geometry and shape semantics in the prediction process.

The method first produces an orientation hypothesis through SO(3)-equivariant learning based on geometry. Equivariance means that the hypothesis responds predictably when the input is rotated. A second component uses shape semantics to predict an SO(3)-invariant residual rotation, which calibrates the initial hypothesis. The residual is invariant to input rotation, allowing the two components to contribute different kinds of information to the final orientation.

Experiments report superior stability and consistency for the resulting predictions. The method also achieves state-of-the-art performance when used for point-cloud part segmentation with randomly rotated inputs. This downstream result shows that the orientation procedure can benefit a task beyond orientation prediction itself. The contribution is the coordinated use of rotation-responsive geometric reasoning and rotation-invariant semantic correction.
icml-2023-stable-and-consistent-predicti.tldr: Combining a rotation-equivariant geometric hypothesis with an invariant semantic correction improves 3D orientation stability, consistency, and rotated-input segmentation.

paragraphs: Latent factor analysis explains observed variables through underlying factors, but learning its structure presents several difficulties. Existing approaches may require the factor count in advance, lack structural guarantees, or leave parameters ambiguous because rotating the latent representation preserves the likelihood. This paper proposes correlation thresholding to learn both the number of factors and a rotationally identifiable structure.

The algorithm builds a graph by thresholding correlations between observed variables. It then translates structure learning into a search for particular groups called independent maximal cliques. This reformulation makes the observed correlation graph the main object of analysis. The authors report that their clique-search technique handles thousands of variables, at scales where competing approaches take impractical amounts of time.

The paper establishes a finite-sample error bound and high-dimensional consistency for structure recovery. Simulations and a real-data example show accurate recovery and empirical robustness when assumptions are violated. The theoretical guarantees and robustness experiments provide different kinds of support: the former characterize recovery formally, while the latter examine behavior beyond the assumptions in tested cases.
icml-2023-structure-learning-of-latent-f.tldr: Searching cliques in a thresholded correlation graph learns latent-factor counts and identifiable structures with theoretical guarantees and favorable scaling.

paragraphs: Finding genes associated with cancer-patient survival can help identify candidates with prognostic value. The task is difficult because genetic datasets have many dimensions and studies often lack an appropriate low-risk comparison group. SurProGenes combines representation learning and statistical analysis to make candidate-gene identification more manageable.

The framework uses a mechanism derived from collaborative filtering to represent patients in an order reflecting survival risk. This ordering supports dividing patients into two groups for comparison. A second mechanism organizes embedded gene vectors toward the ends or centers of reference axes to facilitate recommendations. The learned representations therefore serve both patient grouping and the organization of gene candidates.

To reduce the amount of analysis, the method examines a few representative genes from each cluster. This focuses statistical work on a smaller collection while using the broader representation to organize the search. The authors demonstrate the framework’s potential for identifying prognostic genes. The stated outcome concerns candidate identification and efficient analysis, with possible treatment relevance motivating the work rather than constituting a demonstrated clinical benefit.
icml-2023-surprogenes-survival-risk-orde.tldr: SurProGenes organizes patients by survival risk and genes into learned groups to support efficient identification of candidate prognostic genes.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows can estimate probability densities and generate data, but their usual training methods assume that observations are independent. Real datasets can violate that assumption. When observations depend on one another, treating them as independent may distort the learned density and the samples produced by the model.

This paper changes the likelihood objective so that dependencies between observations are included in training. The authors derive a flexible, efficient learning algorithm that can accommodate different dependency structures. The intervention is therefore in how evidence from the dataset enters the training objective: relationships between data points become part of the statistical model used for learning.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that respecting these dependencies can improve empirical results. In a downstream genome-wide association application, it also produces higher statistical power. This connects the training change to a practical statistical benefit beyond density estimation alone. The findings support accounting for dependencies when they are present, rather than assuming that more complex relationships between observations can be ignored without consequence.
icml-2023-training-normalizing-flows-fro.tldr: A dependency-aware likelihood lets normalizing flows learn from correlated observations, improving reported results and downstream association-study power.

paragraphs: Multistage stochastic programming handles sequences of decisions under uncertainty. Common stagewise decomposition methods become increasingly expensive as subproblems grow or more problems must be solved. This paper introduces TranSDDP, a Transformer-based method intended to reduce the computational burden of constructing the value-function approximations used in that process.

Traditional approaches, including stochastic dual dynamic programming, build piecewise linear convex approximations by accumulating subgradient cutting planes. These planes come from primal and dual solutions of stagewise subproblems. TranSDDP uses a Transformer to integrate cutting planes sequentially. It therefore applies learned sequence processing to the construction of the approximation while retaining a piecewise linear representation of the value function.

Numerical experiments show that TranSDDP efficiently generates these approximations and significantly reduces computation time while preserving solution quality. The result matters because the desired improvement is faster optimization with useful solutions, rather than speed alone. In the evaluated problems, the Transformer-based construction achieves that combination, supporting its potential for handling large multistage stochastic optimization problems.
icml-2023-transformer-based-stagewise-de.tldr: TranSDDP uses a Transformer to construct cutting-plane value approximations, reducing computation time while preserving solution quality in experiments.

paragraphs: Popular versions of Nesterov’s accelerated gradient method treat convex and strongly convex objectives separately. This paper develops a framework that brings those cases together across three descriptions: Lagrangians, continuous-time ordinary differential equations, and discrete optimization algorithms. The aim is to explain and connect methods that are usually presented in distinct forms.

A simple momentum algorithm called unified AGM emerges as a special case. It bridges the two popular accelerated methods and has a stronger convergence guarantee than existing algorithms for objectives that are not strongly convex. The authors also identify practical relevance for ill-conditioned strongly convex objectives with a small strong-convexity parameter, where the distinction between the two regimes is especially consequential.

The framework extends beyond this basic algorithm to higher-order, non-Euclidean optimization, along with a corresponding differential-equation model. It also produces unified AGM-G, an ODE designed to minimize the gradient norm of strongly convex functions. Together, these results make the framework a basis for connecting acceleration regimes and constructing further optimization dynamics with different targets.
icml-2023-unifying-nesterovs-accelerated.tldr: A unified framework connects convex and strongly convex acceleration, yielding a momentum method with improved guarantees and extensions to broader optimization settings.
